phrases.text: You're looking at 27 British ships charging 33 French and Spanish warships, in 1805. By sunset, Britain had lost none. What did Nelson know?
October 21, 1805. Off Cape Trafalgar, on the southern coast of Spain.
This is the Battle of Trafalgar. What happened, and why it happened at all.
Two years earlier, Europe is at war again. Napoleon Bonaparte commands the strongest army on the continent. Only one thing stands between him and Britain: the Royal Navy.
At Boulogne, on the French coast, Napoleon gathers an invasion army and a fleet of flat-bottomed barges. All he needs is control of the English Channel.
But British warships blockade the French ports. The French fleets are trapped, at Toulon and at Brest.
So Napoleon makes a plan. His fleets will slip out, cross the Atlantic to the Caribbean, lure the British away, then race back together and sweep the Channel clear.
The man given that job is Vice-Admiral Pierre-Charles Villeneuve. Seven years earlier, he escaped when Nelson destroyed a French fleet at the Nile. He has no wish to face him again.
In the spring of 1805, Villeneuve slips out of Toulon and crosses the Atlantic. Nelson chases him to the West Indies, and back.
Off northern Spain, a British squadron catches the combined fleet. The fight is inconclusive.
Napoleon orders Villeneuve north, to Brest. Instead, afraid the British are watching, he turns south, to the Spanish port of Cádiz.
At Boulogne, Napoleon's army waits for a fleet that never comes. On August 25, it marches away, east, to fight Austria. The invasion of Britain is off.
Remember that. Trafalgar did not stop the invasion. It was already cancelled. What Trafalgar decided was something bigger.
Nelson takes command off Cádiz at the end of September. He keeps his main fleet about 50 miles out to sea, out of sight, with fast frigates watching the harbour.
Inside, the combined fleet is struggling. Supplies are short. The ships are more than 2,000 men short of full crews, and many sailors have barely been to sea.
Then Napoleon orders Villeneuve to sail for Naples. And on October 18, Villeneuve learns something worse: another admiral is on his way to replace him.
Rather than be disgraced, he puts to sea. On October 20, 33 ships of the line leave Cádiz. Only days earlier, his own captains had voted to stay in port.
In those days, fleets fought in two long lines, side by side, trading broadsides until one gave up. It was orderly. It was safe. And it rarely destroyed anyone.
Nelson had a different idea. Over dinners aboard his flagship, HMS Victory, he explained it to his captains.

His fleet would form two columns and sail straight at the enemy line, at a right angle. They would break through it in two places, cut it into three pieces, and crush the centre and rear before the front could turn back to help.
The risk was huge. Sailing head-on, the leading British ships could not fire back. For a long time, they would just be targets.
Villeneuve guessed Nelson might try exactly this. But his crews were too inexperienced for anything clever. He kept the single line.
Dawn, October 21. The wind is light. From Victory, the British can see the enemy: a long line of sails, stretching for miles.
At eight o'clock, Villeneuve orders his whole fleet to turn back toward Cádiz. In the light wind, the turn takes hours, and his line bends into a ragged curve.

The British form two columns. Nelson leads one, in Victory. His second in command, Cuthbert Collingwood, leads the other, in the Royal Sovereign. Nelson has 27 ships of the line, more than 2,000 cannon, and 17,000 men.

At a quarter to noon, Nelson asks his signal officer to send a message: "England confides that every man will do his duty." The officer suggests one change. "Expects." It's quicker to signal. Nelson agrees.
"England expects that every man will do his duty." Then one more signal: "Engage the enemy more closely."
At noon, the first shot is fired at the Royal Sovereign. Collingwood turns to his officers. "Now, gentlemen, let us do something today which the world may talk of hereafter."
Royal Sovereign, faster than the rest, smashes into the enemy line alone, and fires a broadside straight through the stern of a Spanish flagship.
Behind her, HMS Belleisle is shot to pieces. Every mast is gone. She cannot steer. But she keeps her flag flying, for 45 minutes, until help arrives.
To the north, Victory sails into the fire of four ships at once. For 40 minutes, she cannot fire back. Her wheel is shot away. Sailors steer her from below.
Then she passes behind the French flagship, Bucentaure, and fires a broadside down the length of her decks.
Victory locks together with another French ship, the Redoutable. Its crew gathers to board.

High in the Redoutable's rigging, a French marksman is firing down onto Victory's deck. At about a quarter past one, a musket ball hits Nelson in the shoulder, passes through his lung, and lodges in his spine.
"They have done it at last, Hardy," he says. "My backbone is shot through." He is carried below.
On deck, the French are about to board. Then HMS Temeraire comes alongside the Redoutable, and fires straight into the crowd of boarders.
At five to two, the Redoutable surrenders. Of 643 men, 99 can still fight.
One by one, the enemy centre and rear are surrounded. The French flagship Bucentaure surrenders. Villeneuve is taken prisoner.
The Santísima Trinidad, the most heavily armed warship in the world, with 130 guns, holds out for three hours, then strikes her colours.

The Spanish fought bravely. Two of their captains, Churruca and Alcalá Galiano, were killed on their own decks. The front of the enemy line, which could have turned to help, fires a few shots, and sails away.
Late in the afternoon, the French ship Achille catches fire, and explodes.
Below decks, Nelson hears the cheering. Hardy tells him the victory is complete. "Thank God I have done my duty," he murmurs. At half past four, he dies.
Nelson had ordered the fleet to anchor. A storm was coming. That night, it hit.

For a week, a gale tore at the shattered ships. Many of the captured prizes sank or were driven onto the rocks. Some were retaken by their own prisoners. In the end, the British burned or sank several prizes themselves, even the giant Santísima Trinidad.
Collingwood wrote that he would rather fight another battle than pass through such a week again.
The count. Britain lost about 450 men killed, and not a single ship. The French and Spanish lost around 4,400 killed, and 18 ships captured or destroyed. Only 11 made it back to Cádiz.
Napoleon had won a great victory at Ulm the day before. He kept Trafalgar secret for weeks. When the news finally broke in Paris, the newspapers called it a great French victory.
Villeneuve was released and went home to France. In 1806, he was found dead in an inn, stabbed six times. The official verdict: suicide.
Trafalgar didn't end the war. Six weeks later, Napoleon won his greatest battle, at Austerlitz.
But it settled who ruled the sea. For the rest of the century, no fleet seriously challenged the Royal Navy.
And Nelson came home, in a barrel of brandy, to a hero's funeral at St Paul's.
So, was Trafalgar won by Nelson's genius, or by Villeneuve's fear? Tell me in the comments, and subscribe to Buried Chronicles.
